title: Cloud Service Discovery
summary: Cloud Service Discovery is post-compromise enumeration of the services, resources and identities that a cloud identity can reach. Where software discovery asks what is installed on a host, this technique asks what the tenant offers: compute instances, serverless functions, storage buckets, container platforms, build and deployment pipelines, identity directories, and the logging and security services that record activity. The mechanics are API calls authenticated with a stolen key, token, or role, and the signals live in provider audit logs, which record the calling identity, the action, the target resource, and the result. Providers differ in naming, but the pattern is consistent: a burst of read and list operations across many service types, often including permission denials, issued by one principal in a short window. Graph-style tools chain these calls to map relationships between resources and access paths, which is why breadth matters more than any single call. Defenders distinguish discovery from legitimate automation by profiling each identity: what it normally touches, from where, at what time, and with what tooling. A management platform that lists inventory daily looks nothing like a newly created principal sweeping every service on its first day of use.

beginner.definition: Cloud services are computing resources that companies rent rather than own, such as storage, servers and messaging. This technique is an attacker looking through a cloud account to see what is available. They read the menu of services and note what they might use or attack later.
beginner.whyItMatters: A cloud account often holds secrets, customer records and connections to other systems. Listing what exists is the fastest way for an attacker to find the valuable parts and the weak points. Logging and security services are especially interesting, because disabling them hides later actions. This discovery also produces records, so it is one of the best chances you get to notice an intruder early.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains cloud credentials, such as a stolen key, session token or role.
They call provider interfaces that list resources, including servers, storage and functions.
They enumerate identity and permission settings to see what each account can do.
They note logging, monitoring and security services, and look for ones that are switched off.
They may use a mapping tool that draws connections between resources and access paths.
The provider records these calls in an audit log naming the identity and the action taken.
beginner.example: Imagine a visitor who copies a pass from a caretaker for an office tower. Instead of stealing anything, they walk every floor and write down which rooms are open, which doors have alarms, and where the security office sits. The walk itself is harmless. What they do next is decided entirely by what the walk revealed.
takeaways: Cloud audit logs record discovery calls and name the identity that made them.
Broad listing activity by one account is unusual and worth alerting on.
Permission denials during a sweep often show an attacker testing limits.

objectives: Describe what cloud service discovery looks like across different provider models.
Name the audit log fields that make discovery activity traceable.
Explain how relationship mapping tools turn many small calls into a picture.
Distinguish routine cloud automation from adversary reconnaissance.
Use identity baselines to prioritise which discovery alerts matter.
